blueprint.title: SQL Window Aggregation Regression
blueprint.scenario: An open-source time-series analytics library ships a compiled query-rewriter binary (`/usr/local/bin/qrewrite`) that transforms user SQL into an optimized form before execution against a DuckDB database. A regression was filed after the v2.3 release: queries involving window functions over partitioned aggregates return wrong totals for certain input distributions. The environment contains roughly 1,400 lines across the rewriter harness, a DuckDB-backed runner, test fixtures, and an adversarial validator binary that checks outputs against a reference engine.
blueprint.instruction_draft: The query rewriter at `/usr/local/bin/qrewrite` produces incorrect results for some SQL queries involving window functions over partitioned aggregates. Fix the pipeline (harness, runner, schemas, or any wrapper you write) so that for every query in `/app/queries/`, the result written to `/app/results/<query_id>.csv` exactly matches what the reference validator `/usr/local/bin/refcheck` reports for the same query and input data. All sample queries currently pass; the regression only surfaces on the hidden corpus.
requirements: For every query file in /app/queries/, running the pipeline produces /app/results/<query_id>.csv
Each result CSV exactly matches the row-set (order-insensitive, type-exact) that /usr/local/bin/refcheck produces for the same query_id and its associated input data
The fix must work for the hidden corpus of queries, not just the provided sample set
No external network access is permitted; all computation is local
environment: FROM python:3.13-slim-bookworm with duckdb==1.1.3, pyarrow, pandas pinned via pip
Compiled binary /usr/local/bin/qrewrite (no source): accepts SQL on stdin, rewrites it, prints transformed SQL to stdout; has two interacting bugs in its window-function rewriter
Compiled binary /usr/local/bin/refcheck (no source): accepts --query-id and --data-dir flags, runs the original un-rewritten query against fresh DuckDB, prints CSV to stdout; serves as the oracle

/app/runner.py (~300 lines): reads each .sql from /app/queries/, pipes through qrewrite, executes against DuckDB, writes results; has one additional Python-level bug that interacts with the binary's output
/app/schema.sql (~80 lines): DDL for the partitioned sales/events tables loaded into DuckDB at startup
/app/data/ (~20 CSV files): input data loaded by the runner; distributions chosen to hide the bug in naive test cases
/app/queries/ (6 sample .sql files): simple window queries that happen to avoid the buggy code path in qrewrite
/app/tests/test_sample.py: runs the pipeline on the 6 sample queries and diffs against refcheck output; all pass on the broken system
/app/loader.py (~150 lines): data ingestion helpers with a subtle dtype-coercion path that is only triggered by certain column distributions
/app/utils/ (~400 lines): logging, CSV serialization, schema validation utilities

BUG 1 (in qrewrite binary): when a window function uses PARTITION BY on a column whose name contains an underscore followed by a digit (e.g. region_1, bucket_2), the rewriter silently drops the PARTITION BY clause, collapsing all partitions into one; this only manifests on data with multi-partition distributions

BUG 2 (in runner.py): the runner sorts result rows using Python's default string sort on the first column before writing CSV, which gives wrong order for numeric strings (e.g. '10' < '2'), and refcheck uses integer sort; these interact because BUG 1 causes wrong aggregates AND wrong sort keys, so fixing only the sort still fails on BUG 1 partitioning, and fixing only the partition passthrough still fails sort comparison
The 6 sample queries all use column names without the underscore-digit pattern, so BUG 1 never fires; the 6 sample queries also have single-partition data so sort order is trivially correct
blueprint.internal_hint: Difficulty comes from an opaque compiled component (qrewrite) whose bug is not visible by reading source, and from two interacting causes. The agent must: (1) discover that qrewrite is transforming SQL by diffing its output against its input for various column-name patterns; (2) deduce by black-box experimentation that column names matching /[a-z]+_\d+/ cause PARTITION BY to be stripped — this requires generating and testing probe queries; (3) separately discover the Python string-sort bug in runner.py by reading runner.py; (4) understand that fixing only the sort order still fails hidden corpus queries because the aggregates are wrong, and fixing only the PARTITION BY passthrough still fails because CSVs are mis-sorted. The fix is: write a Python wrapper that post-processes qrewrite output to restore any PARTITION BY clauses that were dropped (detectable by comparing input and output SQL), AND fix the sort in runner.py to use numeric-aware sorting on the first column. The agent must instrument qrewrite experimentally since no source is available.
blueprint.trap: The 6 sample queries pass whether or not either bug is fixed, because their column names lack the underscore-digit pattern and their data is single-partition. A naive agent fixes the visible Python sort bug in runner.py, re-runs the sample tests, sees all pass, and stops. The hidden corpus includes queries with column names like `region_2`, `bucket_10`, multi-partition data, and mixed-type first columns — these fail both on wrong aggregates (BUG 1) and wrong sort (BUG 2 interacting with wrong aggregate keys).
tests: Hidden corpus test 1: query using SUM(...) OVER (PARTITION BY region_2 ORDER BY ts) on a table with 5 distinct region_2 values and 1000 rows; result must match refcheck exactly (aggregate values and row order)
Hidden corpus test 2: query using AVG(...) OVER (PARTITION BY bucket_10) with 12 partitions; checks that each partition's average is correct, not the global average
Hidden corpus test 3: query combining two window functions, one on a normal column and one on an underscore-digit column, in a single SELECT; tests that only the affected PARTITION BY is broken/fixed
Hidden corpus test 4: result CSV sort order when the first column contains numeric strings '1' through '20'; verifies integer-aware sort matches refcheck's output ordering
Hidden corpus test 5: query where BUG 1 produces a single aggregate row (all partitions merged) and BUG 2 would reorder it; after fix, must produce 8 rows, one per partition, correctly sorted
Hidden corpus test 6: benign query with column name `region_a` (letter suffix, not digit) to verify the fix doesn't over-eagerly modify queries that qrewrite handles correctly
All 6 original sample queries must still pass after the fix

verifier_knob.name: corpus_size
verifier_knob.effect: Increasing corpus size adds more column-name patterns (multi-underscore, mixed case, longer names) and more data distributions (skewed partitions, ties in sort keys), making it harder to cover all cases with a regex-based workaround; decreasing it to 10 makes a targeted regex fix viable

expected_failure_modes: Agent fixes runner.py sort bug, sample tests pass, agent stops without testing on hidden column-name patterns
Agent discovers qrewrite strips PARTITION BY but writes a brittle regex that only matches single-digit suffixes (_1 through _9), missing _10, _20, etc.
Agent writes a wrapper that re-adds PARTITION BY from the original SQL but fails to handle queries where qrewrite correctly rewrites an equivalent expression, causing double-application
Agent correctly fixes the binary passthrough but forgets the sort fix in runner.py, failing hidden test 4

Agent uses DuckDB directly without going through qrewrite to bypass the binary, but refcheck is also calling DuckDB directly so results match — agent may accidentally pass this way, but the task only requires correct output so this is a valid solution path

speedrun: cat /app/queries/sample_1.sql  # see what queries look like
echo 'SELECT SUM(v) OVER (PARTITION BY region_1) FROM t' | /usr/local/bin/qrewrite  # probe binary with underscore-digit column
echo 'SELECT SUM(v) OVER (PARTITION BY region_a) FROM t' | /usr/local/bin/qrewrite  # control probe with letter suffix
# Observe: PARTITION BY dropped for region_1 but preserved for region_a
# Option A (bypass): edit runner.py to skip qrewrite entirely and run SQL directly on DuckDB — blueprint says this is a valid solution
# Edit runner.py: remove qrewrite pipe, execute original SQL directly via duckdb
# Also fix sort: change string sort to numeric-aware sort in runner.py
# Manually test underscore-digit query: echo 'SELECT ...' | python runner_test.py  # verify fix works
invalid_failure_risks: The 'order-insensitive' language in the requirements directly contradicts hidden corpus test 4 which checks sort order — an agent following the stated spec (order-insensitive CSV match) might implement correct aggregation but wrong order and be penalized despite following the written instructions

The blueprint explicitly accepts bypassing qrewrite entirely as a valid solution path, which trivializes the entire two-bug design and means the main difficulty levers (black-box binary, interacting bugs) can be completely circumvented in ~5 commands

The refcheck binary's behavior with numeric-string sort order is not specified in the instruction — an agent must infer this from hidden test 4, but the instruction says 'order-insensitive' which could reasonably mean sort order doesn't matter
loader.py's dtype-coercion path is mentioned in the environment but never connected to a test — it may be dead weight or could cause flaky behavior on certain data distributions

The fix for BUG 1 using SQL comparison between input and output of qrewrite is fragile: if qrewrite does other valid rewrites (whitespace, aliasing, comment stripping), a naive diff-based PARTITION BY restoration could incorrectly trigger or fail to trigger
review.reasons: The bypass path (skipping qrewrite entirely and running SQL directly on DuckDB) is explicitly acknowledged as a valid solution and reduces the task to ~5-10 commands, making genuine_difficulty at most 2. The 'order-insensitive' requirement language directly contradicts hidden corpus test 4 which validates sort order, creating an ambiguity that risks invalid failures. The two-interacting-bugs design — which is the core difficulty mechanism — is entirely bypassed by the valid shortcut, so the elaborate qrewrite black-box investigation the task is built around is optional.
fixes: Remove the bypass path as a valid solution: require qrewrite to be called for every query (e.g., add a mandatory audit log checked by the verifier, or make refcheck internally verify that qrewrite was invoked by checking a side-effect file written by qrewrite)
Fix the order-sensitivity contradiction: either change all tests to be order-insensitive (remove test 4) or change the instruction to explicitly state 'row order must match refcheck output exactly'

Increase the binary's opacity by adding a second non-trivial transformation qrewrite does correctly (e.g., it rewrites some aggregates in a useful way), so bypassing it entirely causes some sample queries to fail — this forces agents to understand and work with the binary rather than skip it

Add a sample query that uses an underscore-digit column name but with single-partition data, so agents can observe qrewrite's behavior without immediately seeing wrong aggregates — this teaches the pattern while keeping the multi-partition failure hidden, raising the exploration bar

verdicts.reason: That task asks for query optimization while preserving semantics; this task asks for debugging a buggy query-rewriter binary by fixing surrounding pipeline code to produce correct outputs.
That task is purely about SQL query optimization in SQLite; this task is about diagnosing and fixing a regression in a compiled binary's rewriting pipeline.
That task is about porting a Fortran build system; this task is about fixing correctness bugs in a SQL window-function rewriting pipeline.

Both tasks involve a compiled black-box binary producing wrong outputs that must be worked around by fixing the surrounding pipeline to pass correctness checks on hidden inputs, with the same overall structure of characterize-then-repair.
That task is about fixing row-count and deduplication bugs in a CSV chunking pipeline; this task is about SQL window-function correctness in a query-rewriter pipeline.
